matches.quote: The attribution to about 1.4% Cu²⁺ is taken from Ref. 18, not measured on these crystals, and the same defects may also change n in the visible.
The link between two-dimensional confinement and the anisotropy is asserted, not argued... make clear which ingredient carries the anisotropy.
h-BN (Ref. 24, about 0.7), the obvious UV-transparent competitor, is not plotted.
The authors should measure polarized transmission (and ideally retardance) on thin, polished, oriented plates of known thickness... to obtain α_ab(λ), α_c(λ) and Δn directly in the visible
Fig. 5c shows only faint Cu px/y weight... while Cu 4s, commonly reported at the delafossite conduction-band minimum, is not projected
Fig. 3 itself shows MoS2 and C3H3N3O3·3H2O... with Δn ≈ 2–2.5 above CuAlO2's ≈ 0.6... h-BN (Ref. 24, about 0.7), the obvious UV-transparent competitor, is not plotted.
the slope of ln α from about 1–2 to 3.35 eV implies a characteristic energy of order 1 eV, far from a genuine band-tail value (tens of meV)
The definition also differs from that of the comparison materials in Fig. 3 (rutile, calcite, LiNbO3), whose α is of order 10⁻² to 10⁰ cm⁻¹
A few degrees of miscut or azimuthal misalignment of c relative to s would add further mixing... use generalized or Mueller-matrix ellipsometry to check that off-diagonal conversion is absent
The band-gap values are mutually inconsistent and the Tauc analysis is inappropriate... drop or justify the Tauc-derived gaps.
Surface roughness, a Cu²⁺-rich or oxidized overlayer, and spill-over all reduce and distort the apparent ε2 peak and n, and hence n_ab,max and Δn_max
|Δn|max = 3.67 and |Δk|max = 5.21 occur at the exciton resonance... They should be compared with resonant values... not with the off-resonant birefringence of transparent LiNbO3, calcite or rutile.
The 3.71 eV value is attributed to Ref. 15, which reports about 3.5 eV.
The authors should compute the polarization-resolved dielectric tensor (RPA/IPA at minimum, GW+BSE preferably) and |⟨v|p_x,y,z|c⟩|² along L–F
The claims of "transparency across the entire visible spectrum" and "without optical loss" (abstract, Fig. 3 caption) are contradicted by the paper's own data... and the crystals are black

notes: The figure and reference numbering in the referee concerns (e.g. Fig. S5 for ellipsometry, Fig. S10 for the Urbach plot, Fig. 2e for the birefringence comparison, Ref. 17 for Pellicer-Porres APL 2006) indicates the referees reviewed an earlier draft before the authors added the exciton section (Fig. 4) in arXiv v1. Consequently, C9 (70 degree incidence angle in Fig. S4 caption) and C18 (discussing previously reported excitonic effects as a contributor to anisotropy) were already incorporated in v1. For C18, the review still partly touches on the issue by questioning whether 2D exciton confinement versus the dipole selection rule drives the anisotropy (P9) and asking for BSE calculations (P6). C7 is marked partly because P24 estimates the characteristic Urbach energy (~1 eV vs tens of meV) from Fig. S6 to critique the Urbach-tail interpretation rather than simply asking for the value in meV to be reported.
